title: What a thought experiment is for
dek: A good thought experiment is not a story that wins. It is a device that makes a hidden assumption visible.
speakingPrompts: Invent a thought experiment in one minute about fairness at a dinner table.
When should we refuse a thought experiment because it is too far from life?
Explain the difference between a parable and a thought experiment without using the word philosophy.

blocks.text: Philosophy is often accused of preferring armchairs to evidence. The better charge is more specific: some imaginary cases are so polished they smuggle the conclusion in with the furniture. A thought experiment, used honestly, does the opposite. It isolates one lever — consent, identity, knowledge, harm — and asks what happens if we push it.

Galileo’s falling bodies, Maxwell’s demon, and Judith Jarvis Thomson’s violinist are not novels. They are compressed tests. They say: if you accept A in this stark case, you may already be committed to A in a messier one. The starkness is the method. Strip away the details that usually let us dodge. See whether the principle still looks like something you would sign.

The method fails when the starkness cheats. If a scenario depends on science fiction that changes the meaning of the words (what is a “person” if minds upload?), you may be playing with definitions rather than testing a conviction. If it depends on a single vivid image, you may be measuring disgust or tenderness, not justice. Good practice is to rerun the case with the emotional colours inverted and see whether your answer moves.

blocks.title: A field test
blocks.text: Write the principle you think you hold in one sentence. Then invent a case that makes that sentence expensive. If you immediately add clauses, you have learned where the principle was incomplete. That is success, not backtracking.
Why Curio keeps them on the shelf

Microlearning is not only facts. It is the chance to notice the joints in your own thinking. A five-minute thought experiment will not settle ethics. It can stop you from using a slogan as if it were a complete tool. Take it with you into the speaking prompts: the point is not to win. The point is to hear which assumption you were standing on.
